content: Observational error refers to the discrepancy between the measured value of a quantity and its true value. In the context of statistics, an error does not imply a mistake. Instead, variability is an inherent characteristic of both the entities being measured and the measurement process itself. When randomness or uncertainty, as modeled by probability theory, is attributed to such errors, they are referred to as errors in the statistical sense. For further clarification, refer to the concepts of errors and residuals in statistics. Each time a measurement is repeated using a sensitive instrument, slightly different results are obtained. The standard statistical model for error assumes that it consists of two additive components: systematic error and random error. Systematic error is consistent and occurs with the same value whenever the instrument is used in the same manner. Random error, on the other hand, varies from one observation to another. Systematic error is sometimes referred to as statistical bias. It can be minimized or controlled through the use of carefully standardized procedures. A fundamental part of scientific education involves learning how to properly use the standard instruments of a given discipline. Random error, also known as random variation, arises from factors that are either beyond our control or not controlled during the measurement process. These factors may be too costly to manage, or their influence may be unknown. In some cases, the phenomenon being measured may change over time (as in dynamic models) or may be inherently probabilistic in nature, such as in quantum mechanics (see Measurement in Quantum Mechanics). Random error frequently occurs when instruments are pushed to their operational limits. For instance, digital balances often exhibit random error in their least significant digit.
